thread.title: Finding Out If Your Vehicle Has A Recall Is Very Easy

rewrite.rewritten_title: How to Check if Your Vehicle Has an Outstanding Recall
rewrite.summary: This thread provides a method for checking vehicle recalls using the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). It also discusses limitations and what can't be checked through this process.
seo_outline: Introduction to recalling vehicles and why it’s important
How to use VIN to check for recalls
rewrite.rewritten_article_markdown:
Checking if your vehicle has an outstanding recall is a straightforward process. Members in this thread provide assistance by running their vehicle's VIN through General Motors (GM) systems at work or with other professionals who have access to such data. However, it’s important to note that the system may not have records for vehicles older than 10 years.

TRITON20 initially offered to check VINS and provide recall information but stated he was no longer able to do so due to restrictions at work. Others in the thread mentioned continuing this tradition by working at dealerships, suggesting you can still post your VIN here for others to check if they have access to these systems.

According to TRITON20, running a vehicle's VIN through GM’s system allows checking for outstanding recalls but does not provide information on other service history such as damage from accidents or floods. For instance, he explained that the recall related to tailgate cable replacement was completed in June 2005 under recall number 04007.

Some members posted their VINS and received recall confirmations or negative results. TRITON20 also mentioned that vehicles older than 92-93 might not be viewable due to them being deleted from GM’s data base.

Hi Triton, I have a fuel problem with my vehicle, which has the VIN 2GCEK19TX11289512. I tried messaging you privately, but it seems there was an issue.

The only recall for this vehicle involved replacing tailgate cables in 2005 (recall number: 04007). It affected Yukons and Suburbans from model years 2000-2001. If you receive a new fuel pump from GM, it will include updated wiring. You'll need to connect the body side connector and splice it in for proper functioning. Note that electric fuel pumps often have a lifetime warranty depending on the dealership. The recall addressed issues where wiring overheated, causing poor connections at the fuel tank and erratic fuel gauge readings. Trucks with a similar setup were not recalled.
Could you verify the status of the vehicle with VIN 1GCHC24U61E334394? Specifically, I would like to know which services have been performed on it. Thank you.

Recall #04007 involves tailgate strap replacement. It should take approximately 20 minutes and is free of charge. There have been no warranty claims filed with GM regarding this issue.

Have you heard a definitive answer regarding the intermittent fuel gauge issue on 2004 GMC/Chevy 1500 trucks? The gauge shows empty, then rises when driving before dropping back to empty. Some suspect a bad sending unit at the tank, but others believe it might be an issue with components behind the gauge cluster, as driving and shifting into neutral temporarily resolves the problem.

I'll check in tomorrow morning to see if the gauge is working or not, and whether putting it in or out of gear makes a difference. The few problematic clusters tend to show speedometer issues rather than moving components. Given this, I suspect vibrations, particularly related to the wiring harness near the fuel tank, which was previously discussed. Z71Dook found melted wires due to loose connections getting too hot. If your truck has close to 100,000 miles, it might be wise to replace the fuel pump assembly and the new-style harness and connector for the body-side wiring harness. Typically, fuel pumps last around 100-120,000 miles, so getting a dealer replacement ensures you get compatible parts.
